# Emptiness, Step by Step

*MN 121, the Cūḷasuññata Sutta — set 3, Learning to Look at Your Own Mind*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 12 min · 2,072 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

Ānanda reminds the Buddha that he once said, "These days I mostly dwell in
*emptiness*," and asks whether he heard it right. The Buddha says he did,
and explains what he means.

He starts with the room they are sitting in. This mansion, he says, is empty
of elephants and cattle, of gold and silver, of crowds of men and women.
What is not empty is the community of monks. Emptiness here is always empty
of something, and something always remains.

Then he lays out a gradual practice built on that pattern. Leave aside the
village and the people, and attend only to the forest. What has dropped away
is no longer disturbing you; what remains is a smaller disturbance. Then
leave aside the forest for the earth, the earth for boundless space, and so
on through ever subtler states, each time noticing what is now absent and
what is still present.

At the last step even the subtlest state is seen as something put together
and intended, and so impermanent. Seeing that, the heart is released, and
all that remains is this living body with its senses.

It pairs naturally with MN 122, the longer discourse on emptiness.

## Translation

### The Setting

So I heard.

At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī, in the Eastern Monastery, in
Migāra's Mother's mansion.

Then in the late afternoon Venerable Ānanda came out of retreat, went to the
Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated there, he said to the Buddha:

"Bhante, at one time the Buddha was staying among the Sakyans, at a Sakyan town
named Nagaraka. There I heard and learned from the Buddha's own mouth: 'Ānanda,
these days I mostly dwell in emptiness.' I hope I heard that correctly, learned
it correctly, attended to it correctly, and remembered it correctly?"

"Yes, Ānanda, you heard it correctly, learned it correctly, attended to it
correctly, and remembered it correctly. Both before and now, I mostly dwell in
emptiness.

### The Recognition of the Forest

Just as this mansion of Migāra's Mother is empty of elephants, cattle, horses,
and mares, empty of gold and silver, and empty of gatherings of men and women,
and there is only this that is not empty: the oneness that depends on the
Saṅgha of bhikkhus; in the same way, Ānanda, not attending to the recognition
of the village, not attending to the recognition of people, a bhikkhu attends
to the oneness that depends on the recognition of the forest. Their heart leaps
forward into the recognition of the forest, becomes clear, settles, and commits
to it.

They discern: 'Whatever disturbances there would be dependent on the
recognition of the village are not present here. Whatever disturbances there
would be dependent on the recognition of people are not present here. There is
only this much disturbance: the oneness that depends on the recognition of the
forest.'

They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the recognition of the
village.' They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the recognition
of people. There is only this that is not empty: the oneness that depends on
the recognition of the forest.' So they regard it as empty of whatever is not
there, and of what remains they discern: 'This is present.'

This too, Ānanda, is how they come into emptiness genuinely, without
distortion, and purely.

### The Recognition of Earth

Then again, Ānanda, not attending to the recognition of people, not attending
to the recognition of the forest, a bhikkhu attends to the oneness that depends
on the recognition of earth. Their heart leaps forward into the recognition of
earth, becomes clear, settles, and commits to it.

Just as a bull's hide is stretched out with a hundred pegs until it is free of
folds, in the same way, Ānanda, not attending to whatever on this earth is high
or low, its rivers and ravines, its stumps and thorns, its mountains and uneven
ground, a bhikkhu attends to the oneness that depends on the recognition of
earth. Their heart leaps forward into the recognition of earth, becomes clear,
settles, and commits to it.

They discern: 'Whatever disturbances there would be dependent on the
recognition of people are not present here. Whatever disturbances there would
be dependent on the recognition of the forest are not present here. There is
only this much disturbance: the oneness that depends on the recognition of
earth.'

They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the recognition of
people.' They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the recognition
of the forest. There is only this that is not empty: the oneness that depends
on the recognition of earth.' So they regard it as empty of whatever is not
there, and of what remains they discern: 'This is present.'

This too, Ānanda, is how they come into emptiness genuinely, without
distortion, and purely.

### The Formless Spheres

Then again, Ānanda, not attending to the recognition of the forest, not
attending to the recognition of earth, a bhikkhu attends to the oneness that
depends on the recognition of the sphere of boundless space. Their heart leaps
forward into the recognition of the sphere of boundless space, becomes clear,
settles, and commits to it.

They discern: 'Whatever disturbances there would be dependent on the
recognition of the forest are not present here. Whatever disturbances there
would be dependent on the recognition of earth are not present here. There is
only this much disturbance: the oneness that depends on the recognition of the
sphere of boundless space.'

They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the recognition of the
forest.' They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the recognition
of earth. There is only this that is not empty: the oneness that depends on the
recognition of the sphere of boundless space.' So they regard it as empty of
whatever is not there, and of what remains they discern: 'This is present.'

This too, Ānanda, is how they come into emptiness genuinely, without
distortion, and purely.

Then again, Ānanda, not attending to the recognition of earth, not attending to
the recognition of the sphere of boundless space, a bhikkhu attends to the
oneness that depends on the recognition of the sphere of boundless knowing.
Their heart leaps forward into the recognition of the sphere of boundless
knowing, becomes clear, settles, and commits to it.

They discern: 'Whatever disturbances there would be dependent on the
recognition of earth are not present here. Whatever disturbances there would be
dependent on the recognition of the sphere of boundless space are not present
here. There is only this much disturbance: the oneness that depends on the
recognition of the sphere of boundless knowing.'

They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the recognition of earth.'
They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the recognition of the
sphere of boundless space. There is only this that is not empty: the oneness
that depends on the recognition of the sphere of boundless knowing.' So they
regard it as empty of whatever is not there, and of what remains they discern:
'This is present.'

This too, Ānanda, is how they come into emptiness genuinely, without
distortion, and purely.

Then again, Ānanda, not attending to the recognition of the sphere of boundless
space, not attending to the recognition of the sphere of boundless knowing, a
bhikkhu attends to the oneness that depends on the recognition of the sphere of
nothingness. Their heart leaps forward into the recognition of the sphere of
nothingness, becomes clear, settles, and commits to it.

They discern: 'Whatever disturbances there would be dependent on the
recognition of the sphere of boundless space are not present here. Whatever
disturbances there would be dependent on the recognition of the sphere of
boundless knowing are not present here. There is only this much disturbance:
the oneness that depends on the recognition of the sphere of nothingness.'

They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the recognition of the
sphere of boundless space.' They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty
of the recognition of the sphere of boundless knowing. There is only this that
is not empty: the oneness that depends on the recognition of the sphere of
nothingness.' So they regard it as empty of whatever is not there, and of what
remains they discern: 'This is present.'

This too, Ānanda, is how they come into emptiness genuinely, without
distortion, and purely.

Then again, Ānanda, not attending to the recognition of the sphere of boundless
knowing, not attending to the recognition of the sphere of nothingness, a
bhikkhu attends to the oneness that depends on the recognition of the sphere of
neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition. Their heart leaps forward into the
recognition of the sphere of neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition, becomes
clear, settles, and commits to it.

They discern: 'Whatever disturbances there would be dependent on the
recognition of the sphere of boundless knowing are not present here. Whatever
disturbances there would be dependent on the recognition of the sphere of
nothingness are not present here. There is only this much disturbance: the
oneness that depends on the recognition of the sphere of
neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition.'

They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the recognition of the
sphere of boundless knowing.' They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty
of the recognition of the sphere of nothingness. There is only this that is not
empty: the oneness that depends on the recognition of the sphere of
neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition.' So they regard it as empty of
whatever is not there, and of what remains they discern: 'This is present.'

This too, Ānanda, is how they come into emptiness genuinely, without
distortion, and purely.

### The Signless Unification of Mind

Then again, Ānanda, not attending to the recognition of the sphere of
nothingness, not attending to the recognition of the sphere of
neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition, a bhikkhu attends to the oneness that
depends on the signless unification of mind. Their heart leaps forward into the
signless unification of mind, becomes clear, settles, and commits to it.

They discern: 'Whatever disturbances there would be dependent on the
recognition of the sphere of nothingness are not present here. Whatever
disturbances there would be dependent on the recognition of the sphere of
neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition are not present here. There is only
this much disturbance: the six fields of experience that depend on this very
body and are conditioned by life.'

They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the recognition of the
sphere of nothingness.' They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of
the recognition of the sphere of neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition. There
is only this that is not empty: the six fields of experience that depend on
this very body and are conditioned by life.' So they regard it as empty of
whatever is not there, and of what remains they discern: 'This is present.'

This too, Ānanda, is how they come into emptiness genuinely, without
distortion, and purely.

### The Release of the Heart

Then again, Ānanda, not attending to the recognition of the sphere of
nothingness, not attending to the recognition of the sphere of
neither-recognition-nor-non-recognition, a bhikkhu attends to the oneness that
depends on the signless unification of mind. Their heart leaps forward into the
signless unification of mind, becomes clear, settles, and commits to it.

They discern: 'This signless unification of mind too is constructed and
intended.' They discern: 'Whatever is constructed and intended is impermanent
and subject to cessation.'

As they know and see like this, the heart is released from the sensual outflow,
from the outflow of becoming, and from the outflow of ignorance. When it is
released, there is the knowledge: 'It is released.' They discern: 'Birth is
worn away, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been
done, there is no more of this state of being.'

They discern: 'Whatever disturbances there would be dependent on the sensual
outflow are not present here. Whatever disturbances there would be dependent on
the outflow of becoming are not present here. Whatever disturbances there would
be dependent on the outflow of ignorance are not present here. There is only
this much disturbance: the six fields of experience that depend on this very
body and are conditioned by life.'

They discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the sensual outflow.' They
discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the outflow of becoming.' They
discern: 'This field of recognition is empty of the outflow of ignorance. There
is only this that is not empty: the six fields of experience that depend on
this very body and are conditioned by life.' So they regard it as empty of
whatever is not there, and of what remains they discern: 'This is present.'

This too, Ānanda, is how they come into emptiness genuinely, without
distortion, purely, and in the highest and unsurpassed way.

### The Highest Emptiness

Ānanda, whatever samaṇas or brahmins in the past entered and remained in the
pure, highest, unsurpassed emptiness, all of them entered and remained in this
same pure, highest, unsurpassed emptiness.

Whatever samaṇas or brahmins in the future will enter and remain in the pure,
highest, unsurpassed emptiness, all of them will enter and remain in this same
pure, highest, unsurpassed emptiness.

Whatever samaṇas or brahmins at present enter and remain in the pure, highest,
unsurpassed emptiness, all of them enter and remain in this same pure, highest,
unsurpassed emptiness.

So, Ānanda, you should train like this: 'We will enter and remain in the pure,
highest, unsurpassed emptiness.'"

That is what the Buddha said. Venerable Ānanda was glad and welcomed what the
Buddha had said.

The first discourse is finished.

<dt><dfn>becoming</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;bhava&quot; -- the settling of experience into a way of being that feels like somebody being something. Often translated &quot;existence.&quot;</dd>

<dd>A respectful way of addressing a senior monastic, roughly &quot;venerable sir.&quot; Left untranslated because English has no natural equivalent.</dd>

<dd>A Buddhist monk -- someone who has left household life to practise full time. Left untranslated because &quot;monk&quot; carries centuries of unrelated European associations.</dd>

<dd>Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha&#x27;s usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly &quot;friends&quot; in force.</dd>
<dt><dfn>birth</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;jāti&quot; -- being born, and the link that ageing and dying depend on in the dependent-arising sequence. In MN 141 the word appears once in its everyday sense instead, in a simile about a mother.</dd>
<dt><dfn>body</dfn></dt>
<dd>The physical body, as distinct from speech and the mental side of experience.</dd>
<dt><dfn>cessation</dfn></dt>
<dd>The ending of dissatisfaction and its causes -- what practice is ultimately for. (Elsewhere on this site the same underlying idea is called &quot;quenching&quot; -- both are this project&#x27;s rendering of the same Pali word, &quot;nirodha,&quot; used in different sentences.)</dd>
<dt><dfn>conditioned</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;saṅkhata&quot; -- anything that came about because other things did, and that stops when they stop. Nearly everything is.</dd>
<dt><dfn>emptiness</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;suññatā&quot;. In MN 122 it is a way of dwelling, entered by not attending to any signs.</dd>
<dt><dfn>heart</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;citta&quot; -- the affective or feeling side of mind: the part that takes on a mood, wants, leans, reacts, and can be gladdened, steadied, trained, and released. It is sometimes called the &quot;heart-mind&quot; or &quot;feeling mind&quot;; here &quot;heart&quot; does not mean merely emotion or the physical organ.</dd>
<dt><dfn>ignorance</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;avijjā&quot; -- not general stupidity, but specifically not seeing how dissatisfaction works and how it ends. The first link in the dependent-arising sequence.</dd>
<dt><dfn>oneness</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;ekatta&quot; in MN 121 -- the single recognition the mind rests on at each step, once the coarser ones have been set aside.</dd>
<dt><dfn>outflow</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;āsava&quot; -- a deep-running habit that keeps seeping out and driving behaviour. Often translated &quot;taint&quot; or &quot;defilement.&quot;</dd>
<dt><dfn>recognition</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;saññā&quot; (often translated &quot;perception&quot;) -- the mind&#x27;s act of identifying and labeling what it encounters.</dd>
<dt><dfn>Saṅgha</dfn></dt>
<dd>The community of the Buddha&#x27;s disciples. In traditional recollection formulas, as in AN 11.12, it particularly means disciples who have entered and realized the path, not merely everyone who identifies as Buddhist.</dd>
<dt><dfn>six fields of experience</dfn></dt>
<dd>The six channels through which anything at all is experienced: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and thinking. Often translated &quot;sense bases.&quot;</dd>
<dt><dfn>sphere of boundless knowing</dfn></dt>
<dd>A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on knowing itself without limit.</dd>
<dt><dfn>sphere of boundless space</dfn></dt>
<dd>A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on space without limit.</dd>
<dt><dfn>sphere of nothingness</dfn></dt>
<dd>A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on there being nothing at all to take up.</dd>
<dt><dfn>spiritual life</dfn></dt>
<dd>The Buddhist path of practice as a whole -- not just a set of beliefs, but a whole way of living.</dd>
<dt><dfn>unification of mind</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;samādhi&quot; -- the thinking mind and heart gathered together into one organized, workable whole instead of pulling against each other. It does not mean narrowing attention onto one point. Usually translated &quot;concentration,&quot; which this project avoids because it suggests forcing and strain.</dd>

*[Bhante]: A respectful way of addressing a senior monastic, roughly "venerable sir." Left untranslated because English has no natural equivalent.
*[bhikkhu]: A Buddhist monk -- someone who has left household life to practise full time. Left untranslated because "monk" carries centuries of unrelated European associations.
*[bhikkhus]: Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha's usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly "friends" in force.
*[body]: The physical body, as distinct from speech and the mental side of experience.
*[cessation]: The ending of dissatisfaction and its causes -- what practice is ultimately for. (Elsewhere on this site the same underlying idea is called "quenching" -- both are this project's rendering of the same Pali word, "nirodha," used in different sentences.)
*[conditioned]: This project's rendering of "saṅkhata" -- anything that came about because other things did, and that stops when they stop. Nearly everything is.
*[emptiness]: This project's rendering of "suññatā". In MN 122 it is a way of dwelling, entered by not attending to any signs.
*[heart]: This project's rendering of "citta" -- the affective or feeling side of mind: the part that takes on a mood, wants, leans, reacts, and can be gladdened, steadied, trained, and released. It is sometimes called the "heart-mind" or "feeling mind"; here "heart" does not mean merely emotion or the physical organ.
*[ignorance]: This project's rendering of "avijjā" -- not general stupidity, but specifically not seeing how dissatisfaction works and how it ends. The first link in the dependent-arising sequence.
*[oneness]: This project's rendering of "ekatta" in MN 121 -- the single recognition the mind rests on at each step, once the coarser ones have been set aside.
*[outflow]: This project's rendering of "āsava" -- a deep-running habit that keeps seeping out and driving behaviour. Often translated "taint" or "defilement."
*[recognition]: This project's rendering of "saññā" (often translated "perception") -- the mind's act of identifying and labeling what it encounters.
*[Saṅgha]: The community of the Buddha's disciples. In traditional recollection formulas, as in AN 11.12, it particularly means disciples who have entered and realized the path, not merely everyone who identifies as Buddhist.
*[six fields of experience]: The six channels through which anything at all is experienced: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and thinking. Often translated "sense bases."
*[sphere of boundless knowing]: A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on knowing itself without limit.
*[sphere of boundless space]: A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on space without limit.
*[sphere of nothingness]: A deep meditative state in which awareness rests on there being nothing at all to take up.
*[spiritual life]: The Buddhist path of practice as a whole -- not just a set of beliefs, but a whole way of living.
*[unification of mind]: This project's rendering of "samādhi" -- the thinking mind and heart gathered together into one organized, workable whole instead of pulling against each other. It does not mean narrowing attention onto one point. Usually translated "concentration," which this project avoids because it suggests forcing and strain.
